title: Load Balancers
tagline: The traffic cop that spreads requests across servers, hides failures, and makes horizontal scaling possible.
summary: L4 vs L7, balancing algorithms, health checks, and why it's not a SPOF.

paragraphs: A **load balancer (LB)** sits in front of a pool of servers and distributes incoming requests across them. It's the component that makes horizontal scaling real: clients talk to one stable address (the LB), and the LB decides which backend actually handles each request.

Beyond spreading load, an LB delivers three more wins for free: it **removes a single point of failure** (if one backend dies, the LB stops routing to it), it enables **zero-downtime deploys** (drain a server, update it, add it back), and it can **terminate TLS** and do health checking centrally.

blocks.caption: One stable entry point fans out to a pool of interchangeable backends; dead nodes are routed around.

rows: Full HTTP — URL path, headers, cookies
Dumb & blazing fast; just forwards packets
Content-aware routing (e.g., /api → API pool, /img → media pool)
TLS termination, sticky sessions, rewrites, compression, WAF
More CPU per request, but far more flexible
Microservices, path/host routing — the common case for web

blocks.text: L7 is the default for web apps because it understands HTTP and can route by path/host, terminate TLS, and do sticky sessions. L4 wins when you need maximum throughput or are balancing non-HTTP traffic. Many setups use both: an L4 LB spreading to multiple L7 LBs.

items.detail: Cycle through servers in order. Simple and fair when servers are identical and requests are uniform.
Give bigger servers more turns. Handles heterogeneous hardware.
Send to the server with the fewest active connections. Better when request durations vary widely (some slow, some fast).
Factor in measured latency, not just connection count. Routes around slow nodes.
Hash the client (or a key) to a server, so the same client tends to hit the same backend — useful for cache locality or sticky behaviour without storing sessions on the LB.

blocks.text: Default to round robin for uniform, stateless workloads; switch to least-connections when request cost is uneven. Use hashing when you want the same key to land on the same node (cache affinity). Don't overthink this in an interview — name 2–3 and the trade-off.

sections.title: But isn't the load balancer itself a SPOF?

paragraphs: Good catch — and interviewers love this follow-up. If you have one LB and it dies, everything is down. The fix is to make the LB tier itself redundant: run **at least two LBs** in active-active or active-passive, and put them behind a **floating/virtual IP** (or use DNS / a cloud LB that's internally redundant) so traffic fails over automatically.

In the cloud you usually use a managed LB (AWS ALB/NLB, GCP LB) that is already multi-node and highly available behind the scenes — but you should still *say* you've eliminated the SPOF, because that's the signal the interviewer is checking for.

blocks.text: Always pre-empt the SPOF question: 'The LB tier is itself redundant — two or more LBs behind a virtual IP/DNS failover (or a managed cloud LB), so losing one doesn't take down the system.'

cheatsheet: An LB spreads requests across a server pool — the enabler of horizontal scaling.
It also removes SPOFs (routes around dead nodes via health checks) and enables zero-downtime deploys.
L4 = fast, IP/port only; L7 = HTTP-aware (path/host routing, TLS termination, sticky sessions) — L7 is the web default.
Algorithms: round robin, weighted, least-connections, least-response-time, IP/consistent hash.
The LB itself must be redundant (2+ behind a virtual IP / managed cloud LB) so it's not a SPOF.

questions.prompt: When would you choose least-connections over round robin?
questions.hint: Think about what happens when some requests take much longer than others.
answer: Round robin assumes every request costs about the same — it just hands them out in turn. That breaks when request durations vary widely: a server that happens to receive several slow requests gets overloaded while others sit idle, because round robin keeps sending it more regardless.

Least-connections routes each new request to the server with the fewest in-flight connections, so it naturally avoids piling work onto a node that's still busy with long requests. Use it when workloads are uneven (e.g., some endpoints do heavy queries, others return instantly).
keyPoints: Round robin assumes uniform request cost
Uneven durations overload some nodes under round robin
Least-connections tracks in-flight load and avoids busy nodes
followUps: How does the LB know a backend is overloaded vs just slow on one request?

questions.prompt: You terminate TLS at the load balancer and route /api to one pool and /static to another. Which LB layer is this, and what's a benefit and a risk of TLS termination at the LB?
questions.hint: Routing by URL path requires understanding HTTP.
answer: Routing by URL path (/api vs /static) requires reading the HTTP request, so this is a **Layer 7** load balancer. L4 only sees IP/port and couldn't distinguish paths.

Terminating TLS at the LB centralises certificate management and offloads expensive crypto from app servers (a real CPU win), and lets the LB inspect/route/compress traffic. The risk: traffic between the LB and backends is now plaintext unless you re-encrypt — inside a trusted network that's often acceptable, but for sensitive data you may want end-to-end TLS (re-encrypt to backends) or a service mesh with mTLS.
keyPoints: TLS termination: central cert mgmt + offloads crypto from app servers
Risk: LB→backend hop is plaintext unless re-encrypted
Mitigate with re-encryption / mTLS for sensitive traffic
followUps: How would you do sticky sessions at L7, and why is it usually better to be stateless instead?
